title: Sixteen Thousand Homes, One Krishna
story:
Narada had heard an impossible thing: that Krishna, with a single body, had married sixteen thousand women and kept a household for each. The sage, who wanders the three worlds and is astonished by little, was astonished by this. He came to Dwaraka to see it with his own eyes.

The city itself was the first marvel — adorned, the verses say, with nine hundred thousand palaces of crystal and silver, their streets laid out with care, their squares and marketplaces full of life. But the inner palace was something more: sixteen thousand mansions set with coral pillars and beryl floors, hung with canopies of pearls, lit by jeweled lamps that drove out all darkness, with peacocks calling from the roofs and maidservants moving through the rooms in gold necklaces and fine robes.

Narada entered the first mansion — the palace of Rukmini. There was Krishna, resting on a couch while his queen fanned him. The moment he saw the sage, he rose, bowed, and seated him with honor; he washed Narada's feet and took the water of that washing on his own head — he whom the worlds worship did reverence to a guest. And he asked what he could do for the sage.

Narada spoke his praise simply: nothing in you is wonderful, Lord of all worlds — friendship toward all beings, restraint toward the wicked; you have descended freely for the good of the world. I have seen your feet, the refuge of those fallen into the well of this world. Grant that I may keep the memory of you.

Then Narada rose and went to the second mansion — and there was Krishna again, playing dice with that wife and with Uddhava. "When did you arrive, sage?" they asked him, as if he had just come.

He went to a third, and found Krishna fondling small children in his lap. To a fourth, and Krishna was pouring oblations into the sacred fires, performing the five great sacrifices. To a fifth, and he sat in twilight meditation, chanting the brahman with his speech restrained. To a sixth, and he was riding out among horses, elephants, and chariots. To a seventh, and he sat in counsel with his ministers, Uddhava among them. To an eighth, and he gave adorned cows to the foremost brahmanas. To a ninth, and he laughed at a jest with his beloved. To a tenth, and he sat alone, absorbed in the Person beyond all nature. Elsewhere he made war with some kings and peace with others; elsewhere he performed the thread ceremonies and the weddings of his sons and daughters, and the festivals of his children; elsewhere he worshipped all the gods with great sacrifices; elsewhere he rode to the hunt on a Sindhu horse.

In all sixteen thousand mansions, the same. In every home Krishna was wholly present, and nowhere was he less.

After the first few mansions, Narada stopped being surprised at the sight of him and began instead to test what he saw. In one home the Lord was mid-sentence with a minister; in the next, mid-verse of a chant; and yet when Narada entered, each Krishna looked up as though the sage were the only guest in the world and greeted him with the same complete attention. The same Krishna. The same fullness.

At last he came before Krishna and laughed, like a man who has seen a trick he cannot explain. "I know your yoga-maya," he said, "which even the clever cannot see. Permit me to depart, Lord, to the worlds that are flooded with your glory."

Krishna let him go. And Narada left Dwaraka with his question dissolved. He had come to measure how one man could be husband to sixteen thousand wives, and he had learned that the question was wrongly put. In every home Krishna had been complete; nothing of him had been shared out thin, nothing diminished. The sage walked out of that city with his song already forming in his throat.
reflection: Narada's wonder is the point: he comes to Krishna's sixteen thousand households as a puzzle of logistics and finds the puzzle itself dissolved — in each home Krishna is wholly present, and nothing of him is divided or lessened. The story does not explain yoga-maya; it shows it, room by room, and lets the seeing be the understanding.
next_story_tease: But even as he took leave, Narada knew the wonder was deeper than he could name — and his song of Krishna's glory was about to begin.
hero_scene: Narada stands at the threshold of a pearl-hung Dwaraka mansion and sees Krishna within — playing dice with a wife — while in the palaces behind him the same Krishna lifts a child, pours oblations into the fire, and rides out to the hunt, all at once.
